content: The mixing test is a diagnostic laboratory procedure used to investigate abnormalities in blood clotting. It is particularly useful in distinguishing between a deficiency in clotting factors and the presence of an inhibitor that interferes with clotting. This test is also referred to by other names, such as mixing studies, PT mixing study, PTT mixing study, circulating anticoagulant screening test, PT 50/50, or inhibitor screen. The test is typically performed when a patient exhibits an abnormally prolonged prothrombin time (PT) or, more commonly, a prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT). The goal is to determine whether the underlying issue is due to a deficiency in clotting factors or the presence of an inhibitor that disrupts the clotting process. The principle of the test relies on the fact that coagulation factor levels must drop below 50% of normal to significantly affect PT or PTT. In the test, the patient’s blood is mixed in equal parts with blood from a donor known to have normal clotting function. If the initial clotting abnormality is due to a deficiency in clotting factors, the mixture will have sufficient factor activity (at least 50%) to correct the clotting time, resulting in faster clot formation. However, if the abnormality is due to an inhibitor, the clotting time will remain prolonged despite the addition of normal donor blood. If the PTT of the mixed blood normalizes, this indicates a clotting factor deficiency, and further testing will be conducted to identify the specific deficient factor. Conversely, if the PTT of the mixed blood remains prolonged, this suggests the presence of an inhibitor. In such cases, additional studies, often beginning with a lupus anticoagulant assay, are performed to identify the inhibitor. It is important to note that a prolonged PTT in the mixed sample can also occur if the patient is taking anticoagulant medications such as heparin. In some cases, the PTT of the mixed blood may initially normalize but become prolonged again after a two-hour incubation period. This result is indicative of a factor VIII inhibitor, as these inhibitors typically require time to exert their effect. When this pattern is observed, a specific assay for factor VIII inhibitors is performed to confirm the diagnosis.
